extracted.intended_audience: SEP holders, IP litigators, in-house counsel and telecommunications industry stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Explains how standard-essential patents (SEPs) and FRAND commitments operate in practice, and the litigation and negotiation strategies SEP holders and implementers use across jurisdictions. Covers essentiality, FRAND obligations, injunction vs rate-setting approaches, competition issues, and jurisdictional strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentiality under ETSI guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: A cellular patent is essential under ETSI guidelines where it is not possible on technical grounds, considering normal technical practice at the time of standardization, to implement the standard without infringing that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essentiality is assessed with reference to the technical standard and normal technical practice at the time of standardization. Not every technology in a standard is strictly necessary—some are optional or provide enhanced functionality—so essentiality must be judged on a technical-by-technical basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND commitments (ETSI IPR Policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A holder of a patent that is, or is likely to become, essential to an ETSI standard must undertake to be prepared to grant irrevocable licenses on Fair, Reasonable, and Non-Discriminatory terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This obligation arises from the patent holder's participation in ETSI's standardization work. The commitment to FRAND is upstream (made during standard-setting) and constrains later licensing/enforcement conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND dance / willing licensor vs unwilling licensee test
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking an injunction, courts assess whether the SEP holder has acted as a willing licensor (avoiding hold-up) or the implementer as an unwilling licensee (holding out) — often called the 'FRAND dance', the steps laid out in Huawei v ZTE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts use the Huawei v ZTE framework to determine whether the implementer’s behavior (e.g., refusing a FRAND offer) justifies an injunction. The assessment of parties' conduct—who made reasonable offers, who responded in good faith—can determine relief such as injunctive relief or damages/licensing only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional approach: injunction-seeking vs global rate-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: FRAND considerations differ depending on whether the SEP holder is seeking an injunction in that jurisdiction or seeking global rate setting by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If seeking an injunction, the focus is on parties’ conduct (willing licensor/unwilling licensee). If seeking global rate setting (e.g., in the UK or UPC), the court may consider comparable licenses granted by the licensor to determine the FRAND rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparable licences to set FRAND rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the SEP holder requests global rate setting by the court, the FRAND question may be what comparable licenses have been granted by the licensor – to enable the court to set the FRAND rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts in jurisdictions open to global rate-setting will look at the licensor's portfolio of licenses and comparable deals to infer a FRAND royalty; comparability and transparency of prior licenses are therefore important evidentiary points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition/antitrust issues as tactical vs substantive challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-competitive challenges by implementers are typically used as tactical distractions, with the main focus in most jurisdictions remaining on patent infringement and whether the putative licensee is an unwilling one as assessed by the patent forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outside China, competition complaints usually function as negotiating tools and are generally manageable, often resolved by settlement. China is an important exception where authorities have shown readiness to open antitrust investigations and impose substantial penalties in SEP matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation as leverage in key defendant markets
rubrics_metrics.description: SEP holders increasingly leverage litigation in key defendant markets to establish negotiating positions and secure fair compensation; seeking injunctions in jurisdictions that will grant them is a common strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hot jurisdictions include EU, UK, China, Brazil, and Colombia, with Southeast Asia showing promise. SEP holders select forums by market size and the courts' demonstrated willingness to grant injunctive relief. Global litigation campaigns aim to pressure implementers into good-faith FRAND negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuance: not all standard-specified technologies are strictly necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Although an essential patent means a compliant product will necessarily practice the patent, some technologies specified in a standard may be optional or provide enhanced functionality rather than basic connectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This nuance affects whether a patent is truly essential in practice and therefore has implications for licensing scope and valuation; careful technical analysis is required rather than blanket assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred remedial approach: jurisprudential transplant over prescriptive legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: An overly prescriptive model through legislative intervention would not be helpful from an SEP holder’s perspective; existing persuasive jurisprudence can be transplanted to emerging jurisdictions' pre-existing patent litigation frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerging jurisdictions can adopt established case law principles rather than bespoke legislative regimes; this approach allows flexibility and reliance on persuasive precedents when shaping local SEP enforcement and FRAND adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global litigation strategy goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Global SEP litigation in key jurisdictions aims to pressure unwilling implementers/licensees into good-faith FRAND negotiations, ultimately culminating in a license agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigation is used as a strategic tool to change the bargaining posture of implementers rather than solely to obtain isolated courtroom victories; coordinated actions across jurisdictions can create negotiation leverage.
